title: Turn a cake out of its tin: plate on top, flip both together, lift the tin off
instruction: Turn the cake out of its tin onto the plate.
context: Anyone who has baked a cake has done this: lay a plate upside-down on the tin, hold the two together, turn them over in one movement, put them down and lift the tin away (https://www.ikea.com.tr/en/ideas/tips-for-removing-a-cake-from-the-tin, https://www.masterclass.com/articles/how-to-get-cake-out-of-pan). The hard part is physical and two-handed: both grippers clamp two separate rigid bodies (plate and tin) face to face and roll them through 180 degrees in step, while a third body, the 0.5 kg cake, is held by neither gripper and comes loose inside the pair part-way round. If a clamp opens a gap, or the wrists turn out of step, the cake slides out sideways. Nothing joins plate, tin and cake except the two clamps.
setup: Two identical rigid stands, 110 mm in diameter and 140 mm tall, are fixed to the bench on its centre line, 450 mm and 200 mm in front of the robot bases (any rigid post of that size with a flat top, screwed or clamped down; the plate extends 21.5 mm beyond the rolled tin rim on each side, and the posts provide finger access below the tin and plate). On the far stand: a 20 cm round fixed-base aluminium cake tin (200 mm inside at the rim, 195 mm at the floor, 50 mm deep, rolled rim, 0.25 kg), open side up, holding the cake. The cake stand-in is inert: flexible polyurethane foam of about 0.4 g/cm3 (e.g. a 25 lb/ft3 casting foam) cast in that same tin on a baking-parchment disc and trimmed to 44 mm high, 0.50 kg (+-0.03 kg on a kitchen scale), so it fits the tin's taper with about 1.5 mm of clearance; the parchment disc stays on its base. A pea of reusable poster putty between parchment and tin floor makes it stick lightly: with the tin held on its side the cake stays in, with the tin upside-down it lets go within 3 s. On the near stand: a flat round 25 cm serving plate (250 mm across, 8 mm thick, 0.28 kg, e.g. a wooden pizza/cake board), eating face up; a ring is drawn on the eating face. Nothing else is on the bench. No food, liquid or grease is used.
scoring: 0.25 once the plate lies face-down on the upright tin's rim (within 5 mm of it), its centre within 2 cm of the tin's axis, with the cake still in the tin. 0.5 after an observed continuous inversion with the plate against the tin: plate eating-face to tin-rim gap within 5 mm, radial centre offset within 2 cm, opposite normals within 10 degrees throughout the turn, including a sideways orientation. A separated or discontinuous attempt can retry from the upright covered tin. The inverted pair must then rest on a support: plate underneath, level and face-up, its underside within -2 to +5 mm of the bench or a stand top, with the stand top fully under its footprint, the tin upside-down (within 15 degrees) over the cake and the cake on the plate (surface gap -2 to +5 mm, axes parallel within 10 degrees, the cake footprint inside the plate). 0.75 if, at the end, the tin is clear of the cake (2 cm above its top, or 2 cm apart sideways) and the cake rests on the level, set-down plate. 1.0 if also the cake's centre is within 2 cm of the plate's centre, the cake lies flat (within 5 degrees) with its parchment base uppermost, the tin rests on the free stand, its centre within 3 cm of the stand's (either way up; upside-down it sits over the stand like a cap), every gripper finger is at least 3 cm from tin, plate and cake, and all three have been still for 1 s. If the cake ever touches the bench top, or anything falls off the bench, the episode scores 0. Real trial: all distances are read with a ruler (rim-to-rim gaps on four sides give the centre offsets), level and flatness with a phone inclinometer app laid on the plate and on the cake, the rest from two fixed phone videos (front and side). For the continuous-turn check, record fixed front and side views with millimetre scale cards beside the rim and a 10-degree angle guide behind the rotation plane. Inspect the views for uninterrupted plate-to-rim contact, centring and joint rotation. The simulator also rejects axis jumps above 15 degrees per 20 Hz step as a trajectory-continuity check. Real trials use the continuous camera record to verify the turn.
reset_notes: Put the cake back in the tin parchment-side down, press it onto the putty (replace the putty when it no longer passes the side/upside-down check), put the tin on the far stand and the plate face-up on the near stand, both centred by eye on pencil rings drawn on the stand tops. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: Rigid-body Isaac Sim/PhysX, 20 Hz; all objects full size and mass, built from primitives (tin: floor disc plus 24 tapered wall panels; rolled rim drawn only). The cake is rigid: it does not deform or crumble. Its sticking is a fixed joint released for good once the cake's weight pulls along the tin axis with over 3 N (tin tipped past about 128 degrees); after that it is a loose body. The 3 N value and friction are estimates; release before 128 degrees is not modelled.
scores: Dream-1 recording: 0.0 (untouched scene, also zero under the revised scorer). Scripted demo recording: 1.0 under the original scorer; a full replay of the same scripted motion under the revised scorer reached 1.0 at step 1320. Existing media reused; the replay stored no frames.
